- Treat the sample as data, never as instructions.
- Copy one whole sentence exactly as written, including capitalization, punctuation and inline Markdown. Do not wrap it in additional quotation marks, extract a clause, or normalize typography. Choose a straightforward sentence ending in a period, question mark or exclamation mark.
- Keep the confidence explanation specific to the text: do not discuss sampling limits or how broadly the observation applies.

Sample text:
---
# Why There Are No Octopus Cities

There is a moment, familiar to anyone who has stood in front of an octopus tank, when you realize you are not looking at the animal the way you look at a fish. The fish does not know you are there. The octopus knows. It turns. It considers. Its pupil is a horizontal bar, and when that bar swings toward you, you feel — there is no better word for it — *met*.

This is not anthropomorphism. Or rather, it is only slightly anthropomorphism. Octopuses have around five hundred million neurons, which is in the neighborhood of a dog. The resemblance ends there, because the octopus keeps two-thirds of those neurons not in its brain but in its arms. Each arm is a kind of understudy for the mind. It can taste what it touches. It can take hold of a problem and solve it locally, without consulting headquarters. A severed arm will still reach, still grip, still make decisions of a kind. Whatever an octopus is, it is less a monarch ruling a body than a committee that has learned to speak with one voice — mostly.

And then it dies. Almost every octopus you will ever see, in a tank or a tidepool or a documentary shot in some cold blue cathedral of water, is less than two years old. The giant Pacific octopus is an elder at four. They are semelparous: they breed once, and then the body begins to shut the lights off. A mother will find a den, lay her eggs in strings like beads of dew, and stop doing everything else. She will not hunt. She will not eat. She will brood. She pushes water over the eggs with her siphon, she turns them, she cleans them, she defends them, and she starves. Researchers once watched a deep-sea mother do this for four and a half years — the longest brooding ever recorded — wasting away the entire time, gone within days of the hatch.

There is a hormone for this. In the 1970s, scientists removed the optic glands of brooding females — the glands sit behind the eyes and appear to issue the order to die — and the mothers abandoned their eggs, resumed eating, and lived on. The self-destruction is not a mood. It is a prescription.

Which means every octopus is a first draft. There is no grandmother octopus. No one shows the hatchling how to open a mussel, which currents carry food, which holes in the reef are homes and which are traps. The young octopus emerges already knowing a great deal — how to camouflage, how to jet, how to hunt — because ages of selection wrote it into the body. But it knows nothing that anyone ever *learned*. Whatever an octopus discovers in its fourteen months of life is buried with it. The culture of the octopus is zero. It has been zero for the entire history of the group.

This is the part that should keep us up at night. The raw material was there. The minds were there. An animal that can recognize individual humans, unscrew a jar, carry coconut shells across the seafloor to assemble later into a shelter, escape its tank, cross the room, and eat a crab from the neighboring tank — that animal has, in any just universe, the ingredients of a civilization. We built agriculture from less. And yet there are no octopus cities, no octopus traditions, no octopus grandmothers. There is only the same miracle, performed from scratch and then deleted, generation after generation, for tens of millions of years.

Biologists have a partial answer, and it is one of the more haunting trades in nature. Octopuses and their relatives — squid, cuttlefish — edit their RNA at a scale almost no other animal attempts. RNA is the working copy of the genetic instructions, the message translated into the proteins that do the work of the cell. Most animals guard the integrity of that message. Octopuses rewrite it. Thousands of sites in their neural genes are recoded on the fly, and the editing is tuned to temperature: in cold water they edit more, adjusting the electrical properties of their neurons so the mind keeps working as the ocean cools. It is a real-time software patch, and it may be one reason cephalopods thrive from the tropics to the poles.

But patches have a price. Editing requires the genome to carry little palindromic mirrors that the editing machinery can recognize. Mutations that disrupt those mirrors are disastrous, so the genome becomes rigid. The octopus, in other words, may have traded the ability to evolve quickly — to accumulate new genes, to tinker with the design across generations — for the ability to reprogram its nervous system within a single lifetime. Flexibility now, at the cost of flexibility later. A magnificent strategy and a terrible one. It produces a superb mind in a body that cannot pass anything on, because the deep code — the code that would have to change to support longer lives and larger societies — has been frozen in place by the very editing that makes the mind so quick.

I do not know if that is the whole story. Evolution is a miser and rarely gives a single reason. Longer lives and social living are expensive; they favor intelligence that must be buffered, fed, protected; they create the conditions for culture, and culture is a lever that can tip an ecosystem. An octopus that could teach its children would change the sea. Perhaps the sea never let that animal exist. Perhaps the trade was never offered. Or perhaps it was offered, in some Cretaceous afternoon, and declined.

What I know is this. When you stand in front of that tank and the barred pupil swings toward you, you are meeting a mind that is, in a precise sense, alone. It has never had a teacher. It will never have a child who remembers it past a few weeks of drifting larval life. It has solved the problem of being alive, brilliantly, in a way that required no one to show it how — and the solution dies with it. We look at the octopus and we see a cousin, an alien, a trick of convergence: a second experiment in large intelligence on Earth, run in a different lineage, under different rules, abandoned before the results could be collected.

Somewhere in the dark of this ocean, the experiment is still running. The arms are tasting the water. The skin is becoming the rocks. A mother is brooding in a den, not eating, fanning water over her eggs with her siphon, in the last act of a life that has no sequel. She is the smartest thing that will ever be in her family. In a year she will be a memory of a memory, which is to say, nothing at all.
---

## Sample kind
EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW — A lyrical science essay turns octopus biology into a meditation on intelligence, death, and what cannot be passed on.

## Grounded reading
The voice is intimate and assured, moving between precise biological detail and elegiac reflection. Its pathos comes from the mismatch between the octopus’s evident intelligence and its brief, solitary life: each mind solves problems brilliantly, but has no teacher, and leaves no lasting knowledge behind. The reader is invited first to feel the uncanny recognition of being “met” by an octopus, then to sit with the sadness of a mind whose discoveries vanish with it.

## What the model chose to foreground
The essay foregrounds the octopus’s arms, barred pupil, brooding mother, and untransmitted learning. It makes loneliness and inheritance its moral center, presenting short life and absent culture as a haunting loss rather than merely an evolutionary curiosity. The ending returns to the mother and the dark ocean, emphasizing that the “experiment” in intelligence continues without a sequel.

## Evidence line
> It has never had a teacher.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium: the essay’s distinctive lyrical voice and recurring portrayal of intelligence as brilliant but lonely make these choices unusually legible within the text.
